pages:
Three weeks in, you have learned which stair creaks and which tap runs brown for the first minute. {first} has been teaching you the till every evening after closing. She counts faster than you do, and she is kind about it.

Tonight she stops with a stack of silver in her hand. "The old man used to send me upstairs on the first of every month," she says. "Around this time. He said a supplier was coming and I'd only be in the way. I never saw a single crate."

You ask what the supplier sold. {first} shakes her head and goes back to counting, but she has lost her place and has to start the stack again.

The lounge is nearly empty. Two regulars are arguing about dice by the hearth, and the paper lanterns are swinging a little in the draught from the street door.

Then the draught gets stronger. Nobody knocked.

You can't sleep. The ledger is sitting on your chest where you dropped it, your candle is a stub, and you have added the same column four times and got four answers.

Somewhere below, the pipes knock. They do that when someone has left the bathhouse boiler stoked, and coal costs money you don't have. You put your boots on over bare feet and go down to bank the fire yourself.

There is light under the bathhouse door, and steam, and the smell of the good soap that {first} keeps locked in her own cupboard.

Since Silas Grieve walked in, {first} has been cleaning. It isn't the ordinary kind. She has emptied the old owner's office down to the boards, shaken out every book, and run a butter knife along the back of every drawer.

"Twelve years," she says, when you ask. Her auburn hair is tied up in a dust cloth and there is a cobweb on her sleeve. "Twelve years I thought I knew where everything in this house was kept. I'd like to find out what else I got wrong."

You hear it from the stairs on the fourth day: a crack of wood, a short silence, and then {first} saying a word you didn't know she used.

She comes into your room without knocking. The false back of the office wardrobe is still in her other hand.

You have copied the pages that matter, twice. One copy is under the loose board behind the bar. The other is with a notary on Tanner's Row who thinks it is a recipe book. The ledger itself has not left your coat in six days, and you have started sleeping in the coat.

{first} told you to stay in the back tonight and let her handle the door. You told her no. She looked at you for a while, then went and put on her good dress, the one she wears for magistrates.

pages.text:
It is the first of the month. The regulars know something is wrong. Nobody has asked for a second drink in an hour, and the dice players by the hearth have stopped pretending to play.

{first} stands at the end of the counter with both hands flat on the wood. When the street door opens she doesn't flinch, and neither do you. You're fairly proud of that.

pages:
{first} finds it while she is looking for something else. That is how she finds most things. It is the house's first licence, folded into eighths at the bottom of the strongbox, with a magistrate's seal the size of a saucer and a date on it.

She does the sum on her fingers. Then she does it again on paper, because she doesn't believe her fingers.

"Fifty years next month," she says. "Sam. This house is older than I am, and nobody has ever once thrown it a party."

Word gets out, because {first} tells one regular and the regular tells Old Town. By the end of the week there are flowers on the counter with no cards, and a cask from the brewer with a card that just says 'about time'. There is also one very large, very expensive wreath, sent by a man with a scarred jaw who would like it known that he has moved on.

{first} puts that one by the door, where everybody can see it.

Castle Rosenhal has forty-one rooms. You have keys to thirty-eight of them. {first} says the east tower stairs are unsafe, and she says it the same way every time, in the same words.

But you are the one who signs for the groceries now. The kitchen sends up one more supper tray every night than there are people to eat it. The tray comes back empty, and the napkin is always folded into a swan.

You don't say anything about it. You wait until {first} is carrying the tray herself, late, with a candle, and you are standing at the bottom of the east stairs when she turns the corner.

She stops. Nothing on the tray so much as rattles. Her grey eyes go to the tray, then to you, then to the stairs behind you. For the first time since you met her, she doesn't have an answer ready.

It starts with the Duchess of Aldermere's steward, who comes to look the castle over before his lady will consider a visit. You pour his tea yourself, to be friendly. You fill the cup to the brim. You hand it to him by the bowl instead of the saucer, and then you shake hands with his footman.

The steward is very polite about it. He leaves after eleven minutes.

{first} watches the carriage go from the front steps with her hands folded. She doesn't raise her voice. She has never needed to.

"The small drawing room," she says. "Nine o'clock tomorrow. Bring clean hands."

Lady Seraphine has started coming downstairs. She doesn't join anyone. She stands in the gallery above the lounge in a gown thirty years out of fashion, watches your guests, and sends {first} down with notes: the count is seated too near the fire, the candles are tallow and everyone can smell it, that man is not a viscount.

She is right every time. You have stopped arguing and started moving the chairs.

pages.text:
This afternoon there is no note. A carriage has come up the hill with six horses where four would do, and a crest on the door that makes {first} set down the silver she is polishing.

"Kessel," she says quietly. "He bought up her father's debts the week of the funeral. Stay close to her, sir."

Up in the gallery, Seraphine has both hands on the rail. She doesn't come down. She doesn't leave either.

pages:
The baron hasn't come back. Seraphine hasn't mentioned him, or thanked you, or gone back to hiding. She takes her supper in the kitchen now, at the end of the table, and corrects the cook's sauces.

{first} reports all of this to you with no expression at all. "She asked me how one applies for a position, sir. In general. She was very clear that it was a general question."

pages.text:
Tonight the last guests have gone and the great hall is dark except for the fire. You are stacking chairs, because you still can't watch other people stack chairs.

Footsteps cross the flagstones behind you. They are light and quick, and whoever it is has clearly rehearsed this on the way down. When you turn around her blonde hair is pinned up as if for court. She is turning the signet ring on her finger around and around.

pages:
There is a room in Castle Rosenhal that you had taken for a wall. {first} produces the key from her own chain. It takes her and Seraphine together to drag the doors open, and then all three of you stand there looking in.

It is a ballroom. Dust sheets cover a hundred chairs. The chandelier is the size of a hay cart and has been lowered to the floor and wrapped in muslin. The far wall is all windows, and all of Noble Hill is lit up below them.

pages.text:
"My mother's last ball was in this room," Seraphine says. "I was seven. I was sent to bed at nine and I watched the rest through the banisters." She pulls a dust sheet off a chair, looks at the chair, and sits in it as if it were a throne.

{first} already has a notebook open. You can see columns in it. You can see that one of the columns is prices.

pages:
The first complaint comes from a swordsman with a bandaged knee, who says the big outdoor pool isn't what it was last winter. You put it down to the knee.

The second comes from {first}, and she doesn't say a word. She kneels at the edge of the source pool at dawn with her aunt's old wooden bucket, dips it, and holds her bare wrist in the water while she counts under her breath. She does the same thing the next morning, and the morning after that.

She has also stopped singing. The regulars notice that before they notice the water.

On the fourth morning she finds you in the changing room, stacking towels. She closes the door behind her. Her side braid has come half undone and the red camellia in it is crooked, and you have never seen her leave it crooked.

pages.text:
You have spent the day carrying firewood up from the road, because the carter won't bring his mule past the second bend. Your shoulders ache. Your shirt is stuck to your back. All you want from the world is forty minutes alone in hot water.

There is a board by the door of the outdoor spring, hung with wooden tags that say who has it and when. The tag on the hook says OWNER. You check it twice, because you're that sort of person.

You don't think to check whether somebody has been swapping the tags around for a joke. Somebody has.

pages:
The Golden Crane Inn stands an hour up the mountain road, where the valley narrows. It has a lacquered gate, a gravel garden, and a man whose only job is to rake the gravel. {first} walks through the gate beside you with her chin up and her aunt's bucket under one arm. She hasn't explained the bucket. You haven't asked.

Steam is rising from behind the main hall in thick white columns. There's a great deal more of it than a spring this size should make.

pages.text:
"That's our water," {first} says, quite calmly. "I'd know it anywhere. It smells of iron and it leaves the skin soft. He's bathing merchants in my aunt's water."

A maid shows you to a room with a view of the gravel. Tea arrives, and it is excellent, which makes things worse. Then the screen slides open on a grey topknot and a black coat with a golden crane on the sleeve.

pages:
You wake up because somebody is singing. It is loud and it is off-key, and it is a song about a fisherman's wife that has a great many verses. It's coming from the source pool, and it is the best thing you have heard in a month.

By the time you get down there {first} is already in the water to her knees with her hem tied up, laughing, flinging bucketfuls into the air to watch them steam. The pool is so hot you can't keep a hand in it.

"Forty years," she says, wading out. Her cheeks are pink from the heat. "My aunt kept these springs for forty years. Every spring, when the snow went, she hung lanterns from here to the road and fed anybody who walked up. Soldiers, peddlers, anybody. She said the mountain likes to be thanked."

She wrings out her hem. She is looking at you sideways, and you already know what she is going to ask.

pages.text:
The cold comes down off the peaks early this year. The adventurers on the dungeon road arrive with frost in their beards and stay twice as long, and the Onsen has been full every night for three weeks. Nobody on the staff has had a whole day off since the festival.

{first} has taken to standing in the yard at dusk with her face turned up and her eyes shut. She says she's smelling the weather. You thought that was a joke until this evening, when she opens her eyes, nods once, and starts turning the sign on the gate around to CLOSED.

pages:
Business at {house} is still slow, but it has changed. The guests used to arrive by accident. Now they come on purpose, in nervous pairs, and they ask at the door whether it's true.

It is true. {first} has been rehearsing her entrance on the main stairs all week. She tries it gliding, and drifting, and once coming up through the floor, which made a wine merchant faint. She keeps asking which you prefer. Her silver hair floats around her as if she were underwater, and she is having the best month she has had in a century.

pages.text:
"People are talking about me in town," she tells you happily, from somewhere near the ceiling. "Somebody wrote to a newspaper. Somebody else wrote to a church."

You ask her which church.

She hasn't had time to answer when something hits the front door, hard. It isn't a knock. The second blow takes the latch off.

pages:
Ines left a stack of books on the library table and then made the mistake of telling {first} not to touch them. They are Order manuals, bound in black, with titles like 'On the Bindings of the Restless Dead'.

{first} has read all of them. She can't turn the pages, so she has been getting the candle flames to do it for her, which is why the library smells of singed paper. For three nights you have heard her through the wall. She mutters, and laughs, and once she said "Oh, that's clever" in a voice you didn't like at all.

Tonight the muttering stops. You are halfway down the upstairs hall with a lamp when the air ahead of you goes cold enough that you can see your breath. She steps out of the wallpaper. Her pale violet eyes are very bright.

{first} has missed three evenings. She has greeted every arrival at this house for three hundred years, and now guests stand in the hall with their coats on, looking at the empty stairs, while you make excuses.

You find her in the attic every time. She isn't doing anything. She drifts between the trunks with one hand out, like someone feeling for a door in the dark. Where she has passed, the dust on the floor is rimed with frost.

Ines has started coming up as well. She sits on a crate by the hatch with a notebook on her knee, and she writes down where the frost is thickest and what hour it forms. The silver dagger stays on the crate beside her. On the first night her hand kept going to it. Tonight you notice that it hasn't moved in an hour.

Ines took what you found and rode for the Order's headquarters the next morning. She said two weeks. It has been nearly four.

{first} hasn't mentioned her once. She has, however, found reasons to be in the front rooms a great deal. She rearranges the curtains. She haunts the window seat that overlooks the road. When a rider passes at dusk she goes straight through the wall to look, then drifts back in and tells you it was only the post.

pages.text:
"She won't come back, of course," {first} says tonight, to nobody. "They'll give her a new posting. Somewhere with a proper ghost, one that screams. It's quite all right. I've been left in this house before."

There's a horse on the road. It's being ridden hard, and it turns in at the gate. {first} goes very still, and all the candles in the room lean toward the door.

pages:
Now that {first} has her name back, she wants the rest. She remembers the house as it was: which room was hers, the colour of the drawing room, a pear tree she was fond of. She doesn't remember what came after, and she has decided that she would like to see it.

So on the first dry morning you and Ines take shears and a billhook out into the garden behind the manor. Nobody has cut it back in living memory. {first} drifts ahead of you both, pale in the sunlight, pointing.

It takes most of the day. The pear tree is still there, and it is enormous. Past it, the ivy has grown over something low and square. Ines stops cutting first. She takes off her gloves, clears the last of it away by hand, and steps back without a word.

It is a plain stone. The name has nearly worn away. Someone has scratched a lantern into the top of it with a knife, a long time ago.

It is a normal night at {house}, which means you can't hear yourself think. The dock shift let out an hour ago. There are forty people in a room built for twenty-five, and {first} is working the taps with both hands, standing on the crate she keeps behind the bar so she can see over it.

She is also telling the story. She tells it most nights. Tonight it's for a table of new deckhands: the brewery her grandmother built, the giant who walked in, the bet. "Forty-one tankards," she says, and slams one down. "And I swear on my braids the big bastard was pouring his into his boot."

pages.text:
The deckhands are laughing. Then they stop, and so does everyone else, one table at a time. The tankards on the shelf have started to rattle.

Something very heavy is coming down the street, and it's in no hurry. {first} hasn't turned around. She has gone red to the ears, and her knuckles are white on the tap handle.

pages:
Two ships tie up at the Docks on the same tide: the Gull's Promise and the Black Marlin. You know nothing about either of them. {first} takes one look out of the window and starts moving the furniture.

"Marlin lot by the hearth, Gull lot by the door," she says, dragging a bench. "Their captains fought over a woman or a whale thirty years back. Depends who you ask. Keep the middle tables full of dockers and don't, for the love of ale, let anyone sing."

It works for two hours. The Marlins drink by the hearth and the Gulls drink by the door, and a wall of dockers sits between them, enjoying being useful.

Then a boy off the Gull's Promise, who can't be a day over twenty and is on his fourth pint, stands up on a stool and starts in on a shanty. It has a verse about the Black Marlin's captain. It has several.

You haven't seen {first} above ground in four days. The bar is being run by whoever is nearest it. The cellar door is shut, and there is a sign on it in chalk that reads BREWING. KNOCK AND DIE.

The smell coming up through the floorboards changes by the hour: bread, then honey, then something like a wet dog, then bread again. Every pot in the kitchen has gone missing, and so have your washtub and two of the chamber pots. You have decided not to ask about the chamber pots.

When you finally go down, you take a plate of food with you as a peace offering. The cellar is hot as an oven. There are copper pipes where there were no pipes before. {first} is standing on a barrel, stirring a vat with an oar, with her red braids tied on top of her head and a look in her eye that you have seen on gamblers.

She eats the food without looking at it.

By noon the street outside {house} is full. The dockers have declared a holiday that nobody gave them. There is a man taking bets on an upturned crate, and the odds on {first} are not kind. A fishwife is selling fried eels to the queue.

Inside, the tables have been pushed to the walls. There are two seats left in the middle of the floor: a row of benches lashed together, and one ordinary bar stool. The judges are three harbour pilots who were picked because they can count while drunk.

pages.text:
The rules are the old ones. The drinkers match each other tankard for tankard, and it's the same ale for both. Whoever is last to stand up and say their own name wins. This time a judge watches the giant's boots.

{first} has slept, for once. She has rebraided her hair with every brass ring she owns. She climbs onto the stool, rolls her shoulders, and winks at you across the room.

pages:
The deed to Ironsong Brewery hangs over the bar in a frame that {first} made herself. It is crooked, and she won't let anyone straighten it.

She has spent every free morning since the rematch up at the old brewhouse, scrubbing out vats that had held nothing but rainwater and pigeons for years. She came back each time filthy and furious and happy. Her grandmother's yeast was dead. She found a jar of it in a neighbour's cold cellar, where it had been kept alive for forty years as a favour.

Today a dray pulls up outside with one barrel on it. It has new oak staves and iron hoops, and the Ironsong anvil is burned into the lid. {first} won't let the drayman touch it. She rolls it in herself, up the step and across the floor, and sets it on the bar.

The room has gone quiet. She picks up the mallet and the tap, and then she just stands there and looks at them.
